1xy7eoj:387: The Tencent LEGO project's practice is the first to systematically answer the question: Can AI write code in truly high-risk backend systems? The answer is yes, but with strict conditions. The 13,824 × N combinatorial complexity of the LEGO project is a key metric: it means that after any code modification, the system must maintain correctness across that many dimension combinations; relying solely on human code review can almost never cover it fully. Traditional development flow (human writes code → human reviews → human tests) has a fundamental blind spot in the face of such complexity—human reviewers cannot exhaust all possible interaction paths within limited time. AI's value lies precisely here: it can perform exhaustive risk analysis on every change, turning "what did I miss" from the ultimate limitation of human reviewers into a problem AI can solve systematically. Yet the LEGO practice also reveals the prerequisite: AI must be strictly harnessed within the three-element framework of "context, constraints, and feedback"; otherwise its capabilities become a source of risk.

60o0bh:374: The five-layer Harness Engineering architecture translates the philosophy that "the engineering system is the core asset" into concrete operational terms. The three-layer constraint architecture (permission security base → code rules as compiler → process constraints) builds a defense-in-depth system from infrastructure to operating procedures: Layer 1's permission security base prevents AI from performing operations beyond its authority (e.g., network access); Layer 2's code rules as compiler encodes rules as automatically checkable constraints, rather than expectations described in natural language; Layer 3's process constraints ensure tests cannot be skipped. The key insight is: when AI is harnessed to implement within a single module, a single file, or a single function, the blast radius of its mistakes is controllable; but when AI needs to understand cross-module or cross-level impacts, the error rate rises sharply. This explains why LEGO's five core constraints (such as "network operations strictly forbidden" and "skip if not present locally") look like "restrictions" but are in fact necessary conditions for AI to work safely in a complex system.
a8n7aa:346: Context construction is the core means of eliminating AI's "memory bias". LEGO's four-layer progressive system (Agent.md project constitution → safety discipline → domain knowledge pattern library → specialized Skills) reveals an important law: insufficient AI context cannot be solved by simply "feeding more documents"; it requires structured design targeting AI's cognitive weaknesses. The "safety discipline" layer's approach of replacing "positive preaching" with "counterexample immunity" is especially worth learning—rather than telling AI "you must prevent timing attacks", directly show the contrast between "wrong way (using == to compare passwords)" and "right way (using constant-time comparison)", allowing AI to build safety awareness from concrete cases. The three technical decision questions (What does the RFC say? What does the industry do? What is different in LEGO?) provide AI with a standardized decision framework, ensuring AI's output is not a random pile of "best practices" but a customized solution that truly considers the project's specific constraints.

qfy3z9:398: Adversarial Code Review (adversarial CR) is one of LEGO's most important methodological innovations. Single-model CR has three essential blind spots: knowledge blind spot (different models have different training data, leading to differing understanding of the same code segment), attention blind spot (for diffs over 500 lines, review quality in the latter part drops significantly), and confirmation bias (after finding one issue, the tendency is to continue searching in the same direction). The core idea of adversarial CR is to counter single-model systematic bias with parallel multi-model independent review—model A finds {a1, a2, a3}, model B finds {b1, b2, a2}, model C finds {c1, a1, b1}; after cross-validation, a2 is found by both A and B and becomes a high-confidence issue. This is far more effective than having a single model review repeatedly, and the convergence mechanism (auto-stop when all reviewers find nothing new) is more scientific than a fixed number of rounds. Even more noteworthy is its "debate-style" interaction design—each reviewer not only gives conclusions but also states agree/disagree/maintain; this mechanism exposes the model's thinking blind spots better than static scanning.
rqcerx:136: LEGO's "code rules as compiler" principle reveals a common misconception: writing rules in natural language (e.g., "make sure the code is thread-safe") seems clear, but in fact the consistency of AI understanding and execution depends heavily on prompt quality. tv7mxw:504: While almost all the spotlight on AI Coding is on frontend and client-side work—generating a page, writing an app...—an important question seems to be avoided: can AI write code in backend systems that genuinely "explode" when things go wrong? The Tencent CDN LEGO project is exactly such a system. With 1 million lines of core code and 3 million lines of deeply modified third-party libraries, it serves hundreds of millions of users and shoulders critical responsibilities such as traffic scheduling, protocol parsing, security protection, and cache acceleration. It does not face deterministic inputs and outputs, but rather uncontrollable clients, uncontrollable origin servers, multiple protocols, multiple configurations, and the full public-network attack surface—the combination of these dimensions is not simple addition but multiplicative complexity explosion, with theoretical combined paths up to 13,824 × N. In such a complex system, asking AI to write code means even a single line of error can become an internet-wide incident. But precisely because it is hard, it is worth doing. We systematically explored the path for AI Coding in high-risk backend scenarios: on one hand, we used AI with zero manual code to implement a Rust version of the Nonstop proxy framework, probing the capability boundaries and behavioral characteristics of AI coding; on the other hand, in the ultra-large-scale C++ LEGO project, we built the five-layer Harness Engineering architecture and multi-model adversarial CR, establishing a complete quality barrier for every line of AI-generated code, from generation to production.
